name: functor
intent: Provide one structure-preserving mapping operation per context - lift an ordinary A -> B function so it applies to the value inside a wrapper (absent, failed, repeated, lazy, asynchronous) without unwrapping it - so transformation code is written once per context instead of repeating the open-transform-rebuild cycle at every call site.
problem: A value that lives inside a context - may be missing, may have failed, may be one of many, may not have arrived yet - is transformed by opening the context, applying the function to the payload, and rebuilding the same context. That cycle is repeated at every call site (null checks, try/catch, await, per-element loops), each repetition can get the empty or failed branch wrong, and no helper can be written once against several contexts because the operation has no shared name, shape or contract.
context: Code that must apply the same pure transformation in more than one context: an optional value (Maybe/Option/nullable), a fallible computation (Either/Result/exception-carrying wrapper), a collection or lazy sequence, and an asynchronous or reactive source (Future/Promise/Flow/Observable). It applies when the caller cares about the value inside the context rather than about the context itself, and when the language or its ecosystem can state the mapping once per context - a member method, an extension function, a typeclass instance, or an accessor plus a hand-written helper.
benefits: One operation, many contexts: code that knows only map works on Option, Either, List, Future, parser and stream alike, so helpers (validation, conversion, logging, caching) are written once and applied everywhere.

The context's meaning survives the transformation by construction: absence stays absence, failure stays failure, multiplicity and laziness are unchanged, because the mapper sees only the payload and cannot accidentally drop the structure mid-pipeline.

Refactoring becomes local: map(f) then map(g) is map(g . f), and map(identity) is a no-op, so stages can be fused or moved and a library may replace a chain with a single pass without changing behaviour.

The unwrapping mistakes move out of every call site into the instance: the null check, the try/catch, the await and the index bookkeeping live in one place per context, where they are reviewed and tested once.

It is the price of entry to the rest of the functional vocabulary: Applicative, Monad, Traverse, lenses and effect systems are defined in terms of map, so a context that has it inherits the abstraction layer above it.

Moving between contexts becomes cheap: a transformation written for a plain list keeps working when the list becomes a lazy iterator, a stream or an asynchronous source, because only the context changes, not the mapper.
tradeoffs: Nothing enforces the laws: outside languages with typeclass instances (Haskell) map is a naming convention, so an implementation that maps twice, drops the empty case or reorders elements compiles silently and breaks the fusion and refactoring assumptions of every generic function built on it.

map cannot sequence: as soon as the mapping function itself returns a context the result nests (F<F<B>>) and has to be unwrapped by hand - the point where the abstraction actually needed is bind/flatMap (Monad) or apply (Applicative), not map.
The abstraction only pays off across contexts: with a single wrapper in the codebase the functor is ceremony, because a plain method, an if or a loop is shorter and needs no laws.

Without higher-kinded types the uniformity leaks out through names and encodings: Java says map on Optional but thenApply on CompletableFuture, C# says Select, C++ says transform, and TypeScript/Scala need Kind<F, A> or F[_] wrappers (fp-ts HKT, Cats) before code can abstract over a context at all.

Laziness and asynchrony move cost and timing away from the call: map on an iterator, view, sequence or future often runs nothing until a consumer arrives, so side effects inside the mapper happen later, once per traversal, or on another thread.

Indirection per element: the mapper is one extra closure or function-pointer call per value and strict contexts allocate a new wrapper per map - negligible across a few stages, measurable in a hot loop a hand-written pass would fuse.

participants.responsibility: Carries the extra meaning around the value - absence, failure, multiplicity, laziness, asynchrony - and owns the decision what happens to that meaning when the payload is transformed.
Lifts a plain function into the context: reaches the payload(s), applies the function, and rebuilds the same kind of context around the result without changing its shape.

The ordinary, context-unaware function supplied by the caller; it must be pure, because the context decides whether and how often it runs - never for an empty or failed context, once per element otherwise.

The obligations that make the operation a map: mapping the identity function changes nothing, and mapping a composed function equals composing the maps. They are what licenses fusion, refactoring and generic code above the context.

The per-context definition that supplies map for one concrete type - a typeclass instance, an interface implementation, a stdlib member or extension function - and the place where the laws are stated and tested once.

use_cases: Transforming an optional payload: normalise, format or convert the value inside a Maybe/Option/nullable so the absent case needs no branch at the call site.
Adapting the success value of a fallible computation: map a Result/Either from a transport DTO to a domain object while the error passes through untouched (service layers, parser results).
Mapping over collections, lazy iterators and streams without writing loops: the same mapper applied to an array today and to a lazy or paged source tomorrow.

Converting the payload of an asynchronous result: HTTP clients, database drivers and RPC stubs return Task/Future/Promise/Observable values, and map is how the response shape is changed without leaving the async context.
Writing one generic transformation helper: a validator, cache wrapper, metrics decorator or retry policy written against 'anything with map' and instantiated for every context in the codebase.

Evolving a pipeline's context: moving a transformation from eager collections to lazy views, from plain values to optional ones, or from synchronous to asynchronous code, while the mapping functions stay untouched.

Parser combinator chains: each parser stage returns a value inside a List or Either, and map applies the next parsing function without unwrapping the result — used in Haskell attoparsec, Scala parser combinators, and TypeScript parjs.

Reactive stream transformations: mapping over an Observable, Flow, or Stream to apply a transformation to each event without consuming the stream context — the mapped function runs for each emission, and empty/error streams pass through unchanged.
Validation with accumulated errors: collecting all errors (EitherNel in Arrow, Validation in Cats) where map applies a transformation to the success path while all errors accumulate independently.

Async HTTP request pipelines: an HTTP client returning Task< Response> or Promise<Response> is mapped over with a plain response→domain function, keeping the async context while transforming the payload.

Configuration resolution: loading config values as Optional<T> or Result<T, ConfigError>, then mapping over them to apply defaults, transformations, or environment-specific overrides without losing the absent/failed context.

ML feature engineering: applying a pure transformation function to each element of a dataset or tensor batch (map over a DataLoader or dataset view) to extract, normalize, or encode features without changing the batch context.
Event-sourcing state transitions: applying an event mapper over a stream of CommandResult or Event<T> values where map preserves the envelope metadata while transforming the event payload.

Decorator and middleware chains: applying cross-cutting behaviour (logging, metrics, retry, circuit-breaking) as a map over a context at the edge of a service call, where the decorator wraps the original computation and map transforms only the payload.

Data validation pipelines: using Either or Validation to collect errors, where map applies a normalisation or coercion function to the success path while errors accumulate in parallel via an Applicative (par-traverse) — common in form processing and ETL.
Query building: mapping over an Option<String> to escape SQL characters or apply a regex transformation while None passes through unchanged, building a safe query string without null checks.
UI state propagation: mapping over a React state hook or a signal in a reactive framework (SolidJS, Angular signals) to transform a value while preserving the reactive update context.

ML inference pipelines: applying a normalisation or post-processing function to a model output (Option[Tensor]) or Result[Prediction, InferenceError] without unwrapping, keeping the error path for model failure modes.

Streaming data processing: mapping over a Kafka consumer record, an AWS S3 event, or a socket message to extract or transform the payload while preserving the envelope (topic, partition, offset) in the surrounding context.

Cats' Scala Functor typeclass: a service boundary can map an Option, List or Future response with the same law-governed operation, while Cats' law-testing support checks identity and composition for custom instances.
fp-ts Option pipelines: TypeScript code can use the documented Option Functor and map function to normalize a Some payload while preserving None, then compose the result with other fp-ts combinators.
Rust standard-library dataflow: an Option<T> from parsing or configuration can use Option::map to convert Some(T) to Some(U) while None passes through, keeping absence explicit without a branch.
avoid_when: Only one context type is ever used and it already has a plain method or an if-check: calling that method (or writing the branch) is simpler and needs no laws.
The next step depends on the previous value: that is bind/flatMap (Monad) or apply (Applicative); using map there builds nested contexts and forces manual unwrapping.

The transformation must inspect or reshape the context itself - flattening, choosing a branch from the error value, sequencing two contexts, turning one value into many: that is fold/match, bind or traverse, not map.
The mapping function has effects (I/O, mutation, logging) that must happen exactly once: lazy and empty contexts may skip or defer it, so the explicit control flow is the honest form.

The ecosystem only offers the abstraction through an HKT encoding the team does not maintain (Kind<F, A> wrappers, retired typeclass hierarchies): a consistently named per-type helper is the smaller substitute.
The laws are neither stated nor tested anywhere in the project: an unenforced 'functor' is just a second naming convention, and generic code built on it will rely on behaviour nobody checked.
anti_patterns: Using map for effects: passing a logging, mutating or I/O function to map over a context that may skip it (empty, failed) or defer it (lazy, async), then finding the effect never ran, ran twice, or ran on another thread.
Lawless map: an implementation that drops the empty case, maps only the first element or reorders - it compiles, it is called map, and it silently invalidates fusion and refactoring above it.
map where bind belongs: nesting the context inside itself (Option<Option<B>>, Promise<Promise<B>>) and unwrapping by hand - the symptom that the next step needed the previous value.

The per-type method zoo: mapX/mapY/mapZ for each wrapper with slightly different semantics, called 'the functor' because a folder is named functor; the abstraction exists only where the name and the laws are shared.
Adopting an HKT encoding (fp-ts Kind<F, A>, Cats F[_], typeclass emulation) to map over a single wrapper the codebase already owns and controls.
design_principles: Structure preservation: a transformation acts on the value inside the context and never on the context's shape - absence, failure, count and laziness are data, not implementation detail.
Separation of concerns: the caller supplies a plain A -> B function; reaching into the context, and knowing when not to, is the context's job.
Law-driven design: identity and composition are the real specification of the operation, and instances are interchangeable exactly because they obey them.
Generic programming over a uniform operation: writing helpers against map rather than against a concrete wrapper is what makes them reusable across contexts.
Composition over inheritance: contexts need not share a base type, only the operation and its contract (typeclass or extension-function discipline).
best_practices: Keep the mapping function pure: the context decides whether and how often it runs, so effects inside a mapper are a bug waiting for the empty, lazy or asynchronous case.
Test the two laws once per instance (map(identity) == identity; map(f . g) == map(f) . map(g)) instead of re-asserting behaviour at every call site.
Use the ecosystem's name for the operation (map, fmap, transform, Select) and keep the signature identical across all contexts of the codebase.
Apply map in the middle of a pipeline and unwrap (fold, match, await) only at the edge, where the program has to decide what absence or failure means.
Switch to bind/flatMap/apply as soon as the mapper returns a context; do not paper over the nesting with manual unwrapping.
In lazy and asynchronous contexts state where the work runs: map on a view, iterator, sequence or future defers execution to the consumer, so side effects belong outside the mapper.
Make the laws visible (a small per-instance test suite or a documented contract) so a reviewer can tell a functor from a method that happens to be called map.

In Rust, combine Option::map with the ? operator or and_then for chained fallible operations, but keep map for pure transformations of a known-present value — do not use map when the next step can also fail (use and_then instead).

In Python, prefer toolz.pipe or thread_first/thread_last to chain map operations across multiple types, keeping each step a plain function rather than a bound method — this makes the pipeline readable as a data flow rather than a series of method calls.

In Java, use Optional.map (JDK 9+) instead of Optional.filter for non-boolean transformations; reserve Optional.flatMap for the first step of a chain that itself returns an Optional, and use Optional.map for all subsequent pure transformation steps.

In TypeScript with fp-ts, always use pipe from fp-ts/function when chaining Functor operations so the composition order is left-to-right and matches the pipeline semantics; without pipe the nested function calls read inside-out.

In Kotlin with Arrow, prefer the either { } DSL block for composing multiple Either-returning functions — bind() inside the block short-circuits on the first Left, which is the idiomatic alternative to a chain of .map calls.

In C++, chain std::optional::transform with .and_then to handle the two distinct failure modes: transform for A→B and and_then for A→optional<B>; mixing them up (using transform for an optional-returning function) silently nests the result.

In Go with samber/mo, use result.Pipe2 or option.Pipe3 to build type-safe pipelines that avoid the generic method limitation (Go methods cannot introduce new type parameters), preferring the free functions in sub-packages for type-changing Map operations.

In Scala with Cats, write Functor instances as implicit vals and rely on implicit resolution rather than manual dispatch; test the two laws once per instance using cats-laws FunctorLaws rather than at every call site.

In JavaScript, remember that Array.prototype.map skips sparse array slots entirely (callback is not invoked for missing indices) while still producing a sparse result — use Object.keys or explicit index iteration when all indices must be visited.

In Haskell, the functor laws are not checked by the compiler: write property-based tests with QuickCheck using the standard FunctorLaws to verify any new instance, especially for types with internal state or lazy evaluation.

Nest functors intentionally: use a Compose newtype (Haskell Data.Functor.Compose, fp-ts FunctorComposition) to map over F<G<A>> without unwrapping — apply one transformation across both layers when you have a context inside a context.

Derive Functor automatically where the language supports it: Haskell's DeriveFunctor, Scala's generic with shapeless, or Rust's derive macro for enum-based functors — avoids manual law-verified instances and guarantees law compliance by construction.

In Haskell, write QuickCheck properties using FunctorLaws from hedgehog or checkers to test the two laws for every new instance — the compiler cannot enforce them, and a broken Functor silently breaks every Applicative and Monad built on top.
In Scala with Cats, use cats.laws.FunctorLaws to property-test every custom Functor instance; prefer cats.kernel.instances for standard types over hand-rolling.
In Rust, Option::map and Result::map are the canonical Functor for those types; for custom enum types use a consuming-map pattern (FnOnce self -> Self) and delegate to match.

In Python with the returns library, use @functor from returns.maybe and returns.either to declare Functor instances for custom containers — enables pipe-style chaining across multiple contexts without manually implementing __map__.
In TypeScript with fp-ts, prefer Functor<URI> over a plain method on a class: wrapping the operation in a typeclass makes pipelines composable and enables lifted combinators (flap, void, fproduct).

In C++, when writing a Functor-like wrapper, provide transform (C++23) or map as a member template so it integrates with std::optional and std::variant — std::visit then acts as a generic Functor over variant's map-like overloads.
In Kotlin with Arrow, use either { } DSL with bind() for short-circuiting error propagation; reserve Either.map for terminal transformations at the pipeline edge where the result is consumed.
In Swift, implement Functor by extending your generic type with a map method: func map<B>(_ transform: (A) -> B) -> MyType<B> — the standard library already does this for Optional, Array, and Result.
In Go with samber/mo, prefer Option.Map[T, U] free function over method syntax when building pipelines with multiple type-changing maps, since Go's type parameters on methods are limited.

In a pipeline that spans synchronous to asynchronous boundaries (e.g., a list of futures), apply map at each stage and let the runtime handle sequencing — interleaving synchronous map over a list with async await inside the mapper causes non-deterministic ordering.

When designing a new context type, always implement Functor before Monad: the Functor laws justify fmap and that structure is what Applicative and Monad build on — getting Functor right makes the higher abstractions composable and testable.
